title: Lighting the Inner Lamp
subtitle: The Light of Diwali Within
qtitle: Lighting the Inner Lamp: The Light of Diwali Within
when_where: Sunday 8 November 2026, 11:00 am to 1:00 pm, Ramakrishna Vedanta Centre, New Lynn, and on Zoom. Swami Tadananda, Ramakrishna Vedanta Centre NZ.

quiz.desc: Twenty-five question quiz for the Diwali satsang Lighting the Inner Lamp, Ramakrishna Vedanta Centre NZ. It asks you to understand and apply the teaching.
quiz.og_desc: Twenty-five questions that ask you to understand and apply the satsang.
quiz.blessing: May the inner lamp burn steadily and light the way for others.

questions.q: A friend says: “Spiritual people should skip the Diwali parties and sweets; only the inner lamp matters.” How does the satsang answer?
o: The outer lamp is good and joyful and is part of the festival. The question is whether, as well, we light the inner lamp.
The friend is right: the outer celebration is a distraction that has to be given up before the inner lamp can be lit.
The outer lamp matters most, because the inner lamp lights itself once the festival has been kept properly.
Neither matters; Diwali is a custom that belongs to the past and has no use for sincere seekers.
questions.e: The slide on the two ways to keep Diwali says that lamps, sweets, new clothes, family and friends are “good, and joyful”, and that the inner lamp is “a mind clear enough for the light of the Self to shine through”. The two are not set against each other. The question for the morning is what would make this a year of inner growth.
questions.r: When did a festival leave me with something lasting inside?

questions.q: A student has read many scriptures and can explain them well, yet remains restless. Ramprasad’s last lines in the song say: “my mind has understood, my heart has not.” What does this suggest the student needs?
o: To read more scriptures, since the heart will follow once the mind has understood enough.
To let what the mind understands travel to the heart through practice and devotion, because understanding alone does not yet reveal Her.
To drop the study altogether, since the song says that knowing the Mother is impossible.
To be satisfied, because the mind’s understanding is all that the Mother asks of us.
questions.e: In the Gospel’s English: “But while my mind has understood, alas! my heart has not; Though but a dwarf, it still would strive to make a captive of the moon.” The song does not despise understanding; it admits that the heart is still learning. The Mother is the Inner Self of the yogi, so She is found within, not by learning alone.
questions.r: Where do I understand something with the mind that my heart has not yet taken up?

questions.q: Someone objects: “The verse says ‘I am Shiva, the auspicious.’ That is arrogance.” Which reply is closest to the satsang?
o: It is true that the practitioner becomes divine after enough practice, and the verse celebrates that achievement.
It is only a poetic flourish with no meaning for daily life, so it is best skipped.
It is a prayer asking Shiva to bless the one who chants, not a statement about the Self.
It does not say that the small ego is God. It points to the Self that every being is, the light that is in all.
questions.e: The talk note on the verse says: “‘I am Shiva’ does not mean that the small ego is God; it points to the Self that every being is.” The same verse speaks of the light within, the light without and the light in every being, so the “I” in question is not one person’s ego. (The verse is attributed to Adi Shankaracharya; the English is a free rendering for satsang.)
questions.r: Which of the five lights in the verse is easiest for me to feel, and which hardest?

questions.q: A devotee has practised for years and says: “The light has not come, so I must be unworthy.” Using Gita 10.10 and 10.11, what is the best answer?
o: The Lord lights the lamp only for those who have earned it, so the devotee must practise harder to deserve it.
The darkness is the devotee’s sin, which must be cleared before the Lord will act.
The darkness is ignorance, not a measure of worth; the lamp is lit from within by the Lord out of compassion, and we are asked for devotion and a mind ready to receive it.
The lamp is lit by the devotee’s own intellect, so the answer is to study more.
questions.e: Gita 10.11: “Out of compassion for them alone I, residing in their hearts, destroy the darkness born of ignorance by the shining lamp of Self-knowledge.” Gita 10.10 says the Lord grants the enlightenment to those “ever devoted and adore Me with love”. The darkness is ignorance (ajñāna), and our part is love and readiness.
questions.r: What would it mean to trust that the light is already there, waiting to be seen?

questions.q: One devotee says: “Everything depends on God’s grace, so I need not practise.” Another says: “Everything depends on my effort.” What do the slides on Sri Ramakrishna’s teaching offer both?
o: The first is right, because the Master said that God can be seen the moment His grace descends.
The second is right, because the Master said that a house without light indicates poverty.
Both are wrong, because the Master taught that neither grace nor effort has any part in seeing God.
Grace descends and we light the lamp in our own hearts; neither is left out. The prayer is that He turn the light of knowledge on Himself.
questions.e: Sri Ramakrishna said both: “God can be seen the moment His grace descends,” and “A house without light indicates poverty. So one must light the lamp of Knowledge in one’s heart.” In the sergeant’s-lantern story we see His face only if He turns the light on Himself. Grace is real, and effort is ours.
questions.r: When did I suddenly understand something I had long missed?

questions.q: Sri Ramakrishna said: “The mind will take the colour you dye it with. It is like white clothes just returned from the laundry.” A person notices more irritability after months of constant company that complains. What follows?
o: Irritability is the person’s fixed nature and company has no effect on it.
The mind has taken the colour of what it was dipped in, so company, words and habits are worth changing; the cloth was white to begin with.
Nothing can be done, since bondage and liberation are decided by fate.
The mind is always stained, so the only remedy is to wait for grace.
questions.e: The slide says: “A mind takes the colour of what it is dipped in: company, words, food, thoughts, habits.” The Master’s words are “Bondage and liberation are of the mind alone.” Because the cloth is white to begin with, what is added can be washed away.
questions.r: What is the dust on my own mirror just now?

questions.q: A student wants to produce a spiritual experience by straining harder each day. According to Swami Vivekananda’s image of the mirror, what is the better approach?
o: Polish the image in the mirror until it shines more brightly.
Buy a brighter lamp, because a brighter light shows the image through the dirt.
Clean the mirror: the light does not need to be made, so clearing ignorance and impurity is the work.
Look away from the mirror until it cleans itself.
questions.e: Swami Vivekananda said: “If there is dirt and dust on a mirror, we cannot see our image. So ignorance and wickedness are the dirt and dust that are on the mirror of our hearts.” The slide’s point: the light does not need to be made; the mirror needs to be cleaned.
questions.r: What is the one thing that clouds my mind most often, and what clears it?

questions.q: Gita 5.11 says the karma-yogis work “for the purification of the heart”. A volunteer serves in the kitchen but mostly wants to be noticed and thanked. What would bring the work closer to the Gita’s meaning?
o: Working harder and longer, so that people cannot help noticing.
Stopping the service, since work can never purify the heart.
Keeping the work as it is, as long as the dishes are clean.
Working without attachment, as an offering, so that the work itself clears the heart and not the credit.
questions.e: Gita 5.11: “By giving up attachment, the Karma-yogis undertake work merely through the body, mind, intellect and even the senses for the purification of the heart.” Swami Vivekananda says that “Karma-Yoga is purifying the mind by means of work.” Work done for the heart’s clearing leaves less room for the wish for credit.
questions.r: If purity of mind comes first in the Gita’s list, what would I put first in my own week?

questions.q: The satsang uses two images: dust on a mirror, and noise on a signal (lowering the noise floor). Someone compares themselves to a calmer person and feels inferior. What does the course’s way of putting it say?
o: It is a difference in noise, not in worth; the Light is not what is missing, the clarity of the instrument is.
The calmer person is morally superior, so the other must work to catch up.
Noise means the person has sinned, so the remedy is to repent.
There is no noise floor to lower; it is only a figure of speech.
questions.e: The slide quotes Lesson 3.4: “Neither of these people is morally superior or inferior.” It is a difference in noise. What lowers the noise: meditation, breath regulation, ethical living, the repetition of sacred names, silence and simplicity. Chitta-shuddhi is lifelong and gentle: not self-punishment and not perfection by Sunday.
questions.r: What one thing clouds my mind most often, and what clears it?

questions.q: Which teaching does each image or story carry? Choose one for each line.
rows: White clothes just back from the laundry
Dirt and dust on a mirror
The noise of a busy mind hiding a signal
A sergeant whose lantern shows everyone’s face but his own
c: The mind takes the colour it is dipped in
Ignorance and impurity hide our own image
Grace: we see Him if He turns the light on Himself
Lowering the noise floor so the subtle signal can be heard
questions.e: Sri Ramakrishna’s cloth: the mind takes the colour you dye it with. Swami Vivekananda’s mirror: ignorance and wickedness are the dust on the mirror of the heart. The course’s signal: lowering the noise floor lets the stillness, the witness, become audible. The sergeant’s lantern: we see God’s face only if He turns the light of knowledge on His own face.
questions.r: Which of these four pictures helps me most, and why that one?

questions.q: Gita 14.6 says sattva, being pure, illuminates and is harmless, yet “it binds through attachment to happiness and attachment to knowledge”. A person is proud of being calm and well read and looks down on restless people. What is happening?
o: Nothing is wrong; pride in calm and knowledge is the sign that sattva has matured.
Even sattva can bind: the person has become attached to their own peace and knowledge. Sattva is a window, not the house.
The person has fallen into tamas, because only tamas produces pride.
The Gita is mistaken, because sattva cannot bind.
questions.e: The slide’s plain words: “even sattva binds (14.6): we can become attached to our own peace and to our own knowledge. Sattva is a window, not the house.” The remedy is to keep the light and let go of clinging to it.
questions.r: Which of the three (calm, restless, heavy) do I feel strongest in me this week?

questions.q: Someone says: “I am just a restless person, it is my nature, and nothing will change it.” What does Gita 14.10 suggest?
o: The guṇas are fixed at birth, so the person should accept the nature they have.
Rajas can never be reduced, but it can be hidden from other people.
Nobody is only one guṇa; each rises by overpowering the other two, so which one leads changes with what we feed it.
Only the study of the scriptures changes the guṇas, whatever else the person does.
questions.e: Gita 14.10: “sattva increases by subduing rajas and tamas, rajas by over-powering sattva and tamas and tamas by dominating over sattva and rajas.” The slide adds that what leads changes with company, food, speech and thought (our reading of the verse). Sattva leads upward (14.18).
questions.r: What fed my restlessness or my heaviness this week, and what fed my calm?

questions.q: Gita 14.11 gives a sign that sattva has increased. Which of these is closest to that sign?
o: Feeling nothing at all and wanting to withdraw from other people.
Spending long hours in meditation, whatever the state of mind afterwards.
Winning arguments about the scriptures with more people than before.
The light of knowledge shows through all the doors of the body: in how we see, listen, speak and act, not only while sitting still.
questions.e: Gita 14.11: “When the illumination that is knowledge radiates in this body through all the doors (of the senses), then one should know that sattva has increased greatly.” The slide’s examples: eyes, ears, speech, action.
questions.r: Which of the six marks could I show a little more of by tonight?

questions.q: A colleague is promoted to a post you wanted. Using Gita 12.13 (“friendly and compassionate”, “even-minded in sorrow and happiness”), which response shows a sattvic mind?
o: Being truly glad at the colleague’s good fortune, and letting the disappointment pass without taking it out on anyone.
Congratulating politely while keeping a quiet grudge, which is good enough.
Congratulating loudly so that others see how generous you are.
Avoiding the colleague for a while, since being with them is too hard.
questions.e: Gita 12.13 describes one who is “not hateful towards any creature, who is friendly and compassionate, who has no idea of ‘mine’ and the idea of egoism (‘I’), who is even-minded in sorrow and happiness, who is forgiving.” The slide’s plain pictures include “someone who is glad at another’s good fortune”. The marks are a direction to walk in, not a list to tick.
questions.r: Which one of the six marks could I show a little more of by tonight?

questions.q: You know a true fact that would hurt a colleague and help no one. Gita 17.15 describes sattvic speech as words that cause no distress, that are true, kind and beneficial. What does the verse suggest?
o: Say it, because truth is the only test of speech and kindness has no part in it.
Truth alone is not the whole test; if it is not kind or beneficial, hold it back or find a way to say it that helps.
Say it only behind the colleague’s back, so that the colleague is not hurt directly.
Say something false instead, since that is kinder than the truth.
questions.e: Gita 17.15, as paraphrased on the slide: “words that cause no distress, that are true, kind and beneficial.” Four tests: no distress, true, kind, beneficial. Compare the week’s practice from Holy Mother’s teaching: before speaking of another, ask whether it adds light.
questions.r: If every word I speak were an offering, which of my words today would I take back?

questions.q: Gita chapter 17 and 18 verses name the sattvic form of each area of life. Match each description to its area.
rows: Reverence for the teacher and the wise, cleanliness, straightforwardness, self-restraint, non-injury
Words that cause no distress, true, kind and beneficial
Serenity, gentleness, silence, self-control, purity of heart
Seeing one imperishable Being in all beings, undivided in the divided
questions.e: These are paraphrases of Gita 17.14, 17.15, 17.16 and 18.20 (the English is ours). The Gita calls them the austerities of the body, speech and mind, and the knowledge that sees one Being in all. In 17.16 purity of heart (bhāva-saṁśuddhi) is the Gita’s word for chitta-shuddhi.
questions.r: Which of the eight pictures is already strongest in me, and which did I least expect to find on the list?

questions.q: Gita 18.23 and 18.26 describe the sattvic action and the sattvic doer. A person is anxious before every task and flat or elated after it. What shift do the verses suggest?
o: Give less effort, so that disappointment cannot hurt.
Care only about the result, since results are the only thing that matters.
Do the work as duty with full effort and enthusiasm, without grasping at the fruit, and stay steady in success and failure.
Stop all action, because any action binds.
questions.e: Paraphrase of Gita 18.23: “action done as duty, without attachment, without love or hatred, by one who does not seek its fruit.” Gita 18.26: free from attachment, not boastful, firm and enthusiastic, unmoved by success or failure. Peace is no longer held hostage to results.
questions.r: Where am I working for the result more than for the work?

questions.q: Someone gives up a spiritual discipline because it is bitter and hard at first. Gita 18.37 says sattvic happiness is “at first like poison, at the end like nectar”. What is the sound lesson?
o: Whatever is unpleasant must be good for the mind, so the person should choose the hardest practices.
A practice that is hard at the beginning is always wrong and should be dropped.
Happiness has no place in the spiritual life, so only the bitterness matters.
Judge a practice by where it ends: the serenity of a mind turned to the Self, not only by how it feels at the start.
questions.e: Paraphrase of Gita 18.37: “at first like poison, at the end like nectar, born of the serenity of a mind turned to the Self.” The slide’s note: the verses that follow describe the reverse, the happiness of the senses. Discomfort is not good in itself; the test is the serenity at the end.
questions.r: What practice have I dropped that I might return to, kindly?

questions.q: At a family gathering you meet a relative you find difficult. Gita 18.20 calls the knowledge “by which one sees one imperishable Being in all beings, undivided in the divided” sattvic. How would this knowledge show itself?
o: In treating the relative with respect, seeing the same Being in them despite the differences between you.
In explaining to the relative that you are more spiritually advanced.
In avoiding every disagreement by saying nothing to anyone all day.
In treating the relative as unreal, since only the one Being is real.
questions.e: The slide’s note: “The heart of it: seeing the one in the many, which is the same as seeing the Divine in others.” The Gita’s verse does not erase the differences; the one Being is seen undivided in the divided. This is why seva, seeing Shiva in the one we serve, clears our own mirror.
questions.r: Whom could I see differently this Diwali, and how?

questions.q: In Swami Vivekananda’s reading of the Ramayana (as recorded), who or what is each of these?
c: The Guru, who shows the Lord’s ring
questions.e: Lanka is the body; Sita is the Jivatman, held in it; Rama is the Paramatman, whom Sita longs to be one with; Hanuman is the Guru who shows Sita the ring “which is Brahma-Jnana, the supreme wisdom that destroys all illusions.” Our texts report this as spoken, hence “as recorded”.
questions.r: Which guard am I most often held by this week: rajas, tamas, or my own goodness?

questions.q: Sri Ramakrishna said: “Ravana had an excess of rajas, Kumbhakarna of tamas, and Bibhishana of sattva. That is why Bibhishana was able to receive the grace of Rama.” What does this teach about sattva and grace?
o: Sattva earns salvation, so grace plays no part once a person is good enough.
Sattva and grace are rivals; the more of one, the less of the other.
Only the one born with sattva can ever receive grace; the others are shut out.
Sattva turns us towards the Lord and readies us to receive grace, which then finishes the work.
questions.e: The slide on the Ramayana of the body: Vibhishana, the sattvic brother, leaves Lanka and takes refuge at Rama’s feet. Sattva turns us towards Him, and the grace of Rama finishes the work. Rajas and tamas are guards that keep Sita from Rama until the Guru’s wisdom and grace come.
questions.r: Where in my own life is the turning-towards, and where is the waiting for grace?

questions.q: You catch yourself finding fault with a neighbour. Holy Mother said: “If you want peace of mind, do not find fault with others. Rather see your own faults. Learn to make the whole world your own.” What is a fitting first step?
o: Tell the neighbour everything you see wrong, because honesty is the only way to peace.
Turn to your own faults first and ask whether what you are about to say adds light; then treat the neighbour as one of your own.
Say nothing to the neighbour but speak of the faults to others, so that they are known.
Decide the neighbour is a stranger and have no more to do with them.
questions.e: Holy Mother, five days before her passing: “No one is a stranger. The whole world is your own.” She also said: “The mind is everything. It is in the mind alone that one feels pure and impure.” The week’s practice from the talk: before speaking of another person, ask whether it adds light.
questions.r: Whom could I see differently this Diwali, and how?

questions.q: A devotee meditates for two hours each morning but declines to help in the centre’s kitchen, saying “my work is inner”. Which reading of Swami Vivekananda’s teaching on worship fits best?
o: Inner work is higher, so service is for those who cannot meditate.
Service is higher, so meditation can be dropped by anyone who is busy helping.
Both wings are needed: service in which we see the Divine in the one served is itself part of purifying the mind.
Neither is worship unless it happens in front of an image.
questions.e: Swami Vivekananda: “This is the gist of all worship--to be pure and to do good to others. He who sees Shiva in the poor, in the weak and in the diseased, really worships Shiva.” The slide’s reading: inner stillness without service becomes withdrawal, and service without inner clearing becomes restless doing.
questions.r: One act of seva I will do this month, seeing the Divine in the one I serve.

questions.q: A devotee judges growth by hours of meditation and the number of verses memorised. Swami Ranganathananda asks: “Can you love others? Can you feel oneness with others? Have you peace within yourself and do you radiate it around you?” What is the best response?
o: Keep counting hours and verses, since they are the best proof of growth.
Rank the devotees by their answers to the five questions and encourage the lowest.
Stop asking questions about growth, since asking is itself a sign of failure.
Use the five gentle questions, as a direction and not a score; compare yourself with a year ago, never with a neighbour.
questions.e: Swami Ranganathananda: spiritual growth is “stimulated by meditation, inwardly and by work done in a spirit of service outwardly.” Swami Vivekananda: “This unselfishness is the test of religion.” The slide’s line: no marks, no comparison, a direction and not a score.
questions.r: Which of these five questions would I have answered differently last Diwali?

questions.q: At the end of the satsang a devotee writes ten big resolutions on the Lamp card. What does the satsang suggest instead?
o: Choose one quality, one practice and one act of service, and keep the card in the shrine: three small things kept are worth more than ten promised.
Keep all ten, so that nothing is left out and the year is full.
Skip the card, because writing resolutions makes the mind restless.
Choose three promises for the whole of life, and make them as large as possible.
questions.e: The year-ahead slide gives three lines to fill: one quality to grow, one practice to keep, one act of service to do. “Choose one of each. Three small things kept are worth more than ten promised.” Say one aloud to a neighbour for company on the road, and keep the card in the shrine until next Diwali.
questions.r: One quality I will grow, one practice I will keep, one act of service I will do.

cms.summary: Diwali is the festival of lights, and its inner meaning is the lamp of knowledge in the heart. We begin with Ramprasad's song to the Divine Mother and the verse of the inner light, then ask why the light is not always seen. Sri Ramakrishna and Swami Vivekananda speak of the mind as a mirror and a white cloth; the Bhagavad Gita describes a clear mind as sattva, with its marks in food, conduct, speech, mind, giving, knowing and action. We read the Ramayana as a story of the soul, name seven doors for tending the inner lamp, and look at how we know we are growing. The morning closes with a Lamp card for the year behind and the year ahead, an evening rite for home, a guided meditation and the song Hey Sharde Maa.
reflection_questions: What is the dust on my own mirror just now, and what clears it?
Which of the six marks (truthfulness, purity, inner joy, kindness, compassion, unselfishness) could I show a little more of this week?
Which of the three guṇas, calm, restless or heavy, led my last week, and what fed it?
Which two of the seven doors will I keep this coming year?
Whom could I see differently this Diwali, and how?
